title: Sun of suns, moon of moons
hookLine: the Timeless is praised as the light within every light (Jaap)
tomorrow: Song of songs, dance of dances

lines: THE MOON HAS NO LIGHT OF ITS OWN.
WHERE DOES LIGHT ITSELF COME FROM?
cards: Here's a strange fact about the moon: it has no light of its own. Not a flicker. Every silver night you've ever walked under, every full moon over a parking lot or a lake, was sunlight, bounced.
The moon is a mirror. And the sun? It's burning, yes, but it was formed too, out of something that came before it.
Follow any light back far enough and you start to wonder where light itself comes from. Jaap Sahib asks that with a single doubled word.

teach.b: Late in Jaap, the glide returns, and one stanza is built around doubled words. Namo soorj soorje: salutation to the sun of suns. Namo chandr chandre: the moon of moons.
Namo raaj raaje: king of kings. Namo indr indre: Indra of Indras. The pattern is the point.
Sun of suns doesn't mean a bigger sun somewhere.

It means the sun inside the sun, the light that makes it shine; moon of moons, the brightness behind the reflected brightness. Whatever is greatest in its kind, the One is the source that makes it great.
Then comes a surprise. Namo andhkaare: salutation to the darkness. Namo tej teje: to the radiance of radiances.
Darkness and radiance in one breath: in Jaap, the One is saluted in the night as well as in the bright things.
And it ends: namo beej beeje, seed of seeds, the start of every start. Sikhs hear a close idea in the evening too.

In the prayer before sleep, Kirtan Sohila, Guru Nanak sings that one light is in everyone, and by that light all are lit. The Tenth Guru packs it into a doubled word; the first Guru gives it a whole hymn.
Read this way, every bright thing you admire, a teacher's mind, a friend's laugh, a sky at dusk, is like the moon: lovely, and lit from somewhere else. Jaap bows past the light to its source.

how: Sikhs recite this doubled-word stanza near the end of Jaap Sahib each morning, and hear the same idea of one light in all at night in Kirtan Sohila.

o: the sun; in Jaap, the light inside every light
a fire lit at dawn for morning prayer
the moon, which shines with borrowed light

games.q: sun of suns — tap the pairs.

s: sun of suns means a bigger sun somewhere in the sky
it means the light inside the sun, the source that makes it shine.
the same stanza salutes darkness as well as radiance
namo andhkaare, namo tej teje: darkness and radiance saluted in one breath.
the idea of one light in all also appears in Kirtan Sohila
Guru Nanak sings that one light is in everyone, and by it all are lit.

games.q: you're praising the One, and you've reached the brightest things you know: the sun, the moon. how does Jaap name the One?
o: the sun of suns, the light inside the light.
the maker of the sun, far away.
games.why: namo soorj soorje: the doubled word points to the source within, not a rival light.

practice: Look briefly at a lamp, a candle or a bright window, never the sun itself, then close your eyes and watch the glow that stays behind your eyelids. Let it fade, and rest in the dark, which Jaap salutes too.
If you pray, you can say namo soorj soorje softly.

wordCard.voice: Soorj. The sun — namo soorj soorje, Jaap's bow to the light inside every light, the source that makes the sun shine and the moon glow.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: suraj, the sun; Jaap doubles it, soorj soorje, sun of suns.

carryVoice: Your line: light of lights. Every bright thing is lit from somewhere. Day three hundred forty-two, done.

sources.ref: Jaap Sahib (bhujang prayat): namo soorj soorje, namo chandr chandre … namo andhkaare, namo tej teje … namo beej beeje
